papers.title: Stain-robust classification of Alzheimer's disease and chronic traumatic encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Retrospective reassessment of archival brain banks provides opportunities to identify previously undocumented neuropathologies. However, limited tissue availability and preservation, together with differences in sampling and staining protocols across brain banks, can con-strain the histological information available for analysis. This study investigated whether computational models can integrate complementary information across histological stains and retain discriminative information under incomplete stain availability. A deep learning model incorporating shared-specific feature modeling, cross-stain knowledge distillation, and random modality masking was developed and evaluated on 1, 607 whole slide images from the dorsolateral frontal cortex of 602 donors across three cohorts. Using chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) and Alzheimers disease (AD) and their comorbidity as a proof-of-principle application, our model achieved macro-averaged areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.899, 0.904, and 0.898 across three stain-defined groups, exceeding corresponding single-stain baselines. Discriminative performance was retained when each groups defining stain was withheld. Model-predicted disease probabilities were associated with neuropathological staging measures for AD and CTE, and spatial attribution patterns on the remaining stains were largely preserved under defining-stain masking. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of leveraging complementary and partially overlapping histopathological information under incomplete stain availability, providing a foundation for future computational studies across brain regions and brain banks.

papers.title: Beyond Consensus: Human Ground Truth, Expert Disagreement, and Clinical Relevance in Pathology AI
papers.abstract: Human consensus is often treated as ground truth in clinical artificial intelligence (AI), yet greater agreement does not necessarily ensure greater clinical relevance. We investigated how expert panel size, composition, and consensus formation influence the reproducibility and clinical relevance of reference standards across three independent pathology cohorts evaluated by international expert pathologists: 50 transbronchial lung cryobiopsy cases from patients with interstitial lung disease assessed by 27 pathologists, 95 resected lung adenocarcinomas evaluated by 11 pathologists, and 596 images of pulmonary granulomatous lesions evaluated by 12 pathologists. Larger panels produced more stable collective judgments but did not improve associations with disease progression or survival in the first two cohorts, instead converging toward consensus classifications with weaker outcome associations. Groups of pathologists identified solely by their diagnostic behavior generated consensus classifications with differing clinical relevance. In lung adenocarcinoma, examination of cases graded differently by the all-rater consensus and a distinct pathologist cluster revealed specific morphological patterns potentially contributing to these differences, suggesting that expert disagreement may contain clinically informative signals. In the granuloma cohort, a modified Delphi process increased agreement, with Krippendorffs rising from 0.351 to 0.539, while disease-morphology associations changed only modestly. These findings demonstrate that reproducibility and clinical relevance are distinct properties of expert-derived reference standards. Expert disagreement should therefore not be regarded solely as noise to be eliminated, but also as a potential source of clinically meaningful information. Identifying and independently validating outcome-associated morphological features may enable refinement of existing consensus frameworks, supporting the development of more clinically relevant, task-specific ground truth for pathology AI.

papers.title: Pathologic aggregation of α-synuclein and tau in the gut mirrors the brain, in both Lewy body disease and non-synucleinopathies
papers.abstract: Seeded aggregation of -synuclein and tau in the gastrointestinal tract is a potential biomarker and window into disease pathogenesis, but its quantitative relationship to the brain is unknown. Here, various regions of the gut and brain from autopsies of Lewy body disease and other diagnoses were tested for seeded aggregation of -synuclein and an Alzheimers disease-related tau species, tau-dGAE. Gut seeding of -synuclein (51.8 {+/-} 16.8 vs 112.6 {+/-} 23.0 hours) and tau-dGAE (28.5 {+/-} 2.6 vs 31.7 {+/-} 2.9 hours) was faster in Lewy body disease than non-Lewy cases and was correlated with seeding in frontal cortex and midbrain/medulla (Pearsons r from 0.75 - 0.63). Seeding of -synuclein in gut tissue was also correlated with loss of nigral pigment, pigmented neurons, Lewy bodies, and tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons as well as -synuclein in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (r values from 0.76 - 0.49). Seeding of tau-dGAE in duodenum (but not brain) was faster in Lewy body disease compared to non-Lewy cases (28.5 {+/-} 2.6 vs 31.7 {+/-} 2.9 hours). Tau seeded aggregation in duodenum was correlated with tau-dGAE seeded aggregation in hippocampus and frontal cortex (r values from 0.58 - 0.55) and with tau and amyloid immunohistochemistry in the hippocampus, mainly for cases of Lewy body disease. Seeding for -synuclein and tau-dGAE in the gut correlated with seeding in the brain regardless of disease status. Overall data show a quantitative mirroring of peripheral and central seeded aggregation and neuropathology and demonstrate its utility for studies of pathogenesis and clinical biomarkers.

papers.title: "Independent Predictors of Early Mortality among TB/HIV Co-infected Patients in Northern Cameroon: A Multivariate Logistic Regression and Sensitivity Analysis"
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe concurrent infection of Tuberculosis (TB) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) constitutes a significant clinical challenge and public health emergency throughout Sub-Saharan Africa. Although national healthcare systems provide complimentary diagnostic and treatment services, early-stage mortality rates among individuals with dual infections remain critically elevated. This investigation seeks to determine independent clinical, immunological, behavioral, and geographic factors associated with mortality outcomes in TB/HIV co-infected populations within the Benoue Department of North Cameroon, employing district-level primary analytical modeling supplemented by secondary sensitivity analyses to mitigate potential bias from limited data availability. MethodsA mixed retrospective and prospective cohort investigation was described, encompassing 406 co-infected individuals receiving treatment across all 14 Diagnostic and Treatment Centers (CDTs) distributed throughout the 8 health districts of the department during the period from January 1, 2022, through December 31, 2023, with extension of tuberculosis monitoring treatment ended on November 30, 2024. Statistical analysis conducted using SPSS version 25 incorporated preliminary bivariate Chi-square testing (p < 0.05) succeeded by primary multivariate binary logistic regression modeling and a supplementary sensitivity analysis stratifying geographic location into urban central versus combined peripheral and rural district categories [1-26]. ResultsAmong 3,883 patients initiating tuberculosis treatment, 406 had concurrent HIV infection (10.46% prevalence). This co-infected group experienced significantly higher mortality at 15.02% (61/406), accounting for 84.72% (61/72) of all tuberculosis-related deaths in the department (p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified multiple independent mortality risk factors: geographic location in outlying districts (Gashiga: AOR = 56.81 [1.52-2127.84], p = 0.029; Garoua II: AOR = 48.36 [3.10-755.42], p = 0.006; Pitoa: AOR = 48.21 [2.53- 918.98], p = 0.010; Lagdo: AOR = 28.63 [1.70-481.03], p = 0.020), severe immunosuppression at WHO Stage III (AOR = 9.88 [2.28-42.89], p = 0.002) and Stage IV (AOR = 10.81 [4.77- 24.54], p < 0.001), inadequate medication adherence (AOR = 4.86 [1.14-20.69], p = 0.033), and elevated viral load (AOR = 7.46 [1.73-32.25], p = 0.007). A secondary sensitivity analysis that combined outlying district categories substantially decreased standard errors from 1.849 to 0.485 and generated a precise 95% confidence interval (AOR = 9.40 [3.63-24.32], p < 0.001), confirming that unequal healthcare access in rural areas represents a critical driver of excess mortality. ConclusionThe heightened early mortality in TB/HIV co-infected individuals in North Cameroon stems from geographic variations in healthcare availability, late clinical diagnosis, poor medication compliance, and gaps in viral load monitoring systems. Reducing this mortality requires introducing rapid point-of-care viral load testing, establishing accessible molecular diagnostic facilities across regions, and deploying community-based programs to improve treatment compliance.

papers.title: ZNF683-positive tissue-resident memory T cells organize treatment-refractory niches with targetable circuits in inclusion body myositis
authors: F. V. A. De Los Reyes
papers.abstract: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is a progressive autoimmune myositis refractory to conventional immunosuppression, yet mechanisms sustaining chronic inflammation remain unresolved. Integrating comparative single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and orthogonal validation across autoimmune myositis, we identified ZNF683+IL7R+ cytotoxic tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells with natural killer cell-like features enriched in IBM. Trajectory analysis positioned an early-disease ZBTB16+ cytotoxic T cell state upstream of ZNF683+IL7R+TRM. ZNF683 overexpression induced memory and natural killer cell-like transcriptional programs while attenuating glucocorticoid-response signatures, linking this program to treatment refractoriness. Ligand-receptor modeling nominated candidate targetable circuits involving IL-15-IL15RA, XCL1-XCR1, and HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4. Spatial transcriptomics localized ZNF683+TRM to stress-associated IBM niches. These findings define a disease-specific TRM-centered circuit linked to treatment refractoriness and candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities in IBM. One-sentence summaryZNF683+IL7R+ TRM cells organize targetable treatment-refractory IBM niches involving IL-15-IL-15RA, XCL1-XCR1, and HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 axes.

papers.title: MorphoStain: Physics-Guided Latent Diffusion and Morphological Distillation for Multiplex Stain Decomposition in Alzheimer's Neuropathology
papers.abstract: Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) enables simultaneous biomarker profiling, yet unmixing colocalized targets with identical spectra, such as dual-DAB marking Tau and Amyloid-{beta} in Alzheimers pathology, remains mathematically ill-posed. We propose MorphoStain, an unsupervised, physics-guided framework for morphological stain decomposition with epistemic uncertainty quantification. MorphoStain models stain separation via a conditional Latent Diffusion Teacher operating on a Beer- Lambert optical-density manifold, guided by pathology foundation models. To enable real-time clinical throughput, the teacher is distilled into a FastStudentU-Net (0.12M parameters, > 1,400 x compression), while a Symmetric Morphological Routing Module dynamically disentangles identical chromogen overlap. Evaluated on 9,908 held-out patches from the SEA-AD cohort, MorphoStain achieves 40.56 dB PSNR and 0.9961 SSIM at 140.1 FPS, showing statistically significant gains over InverseAE (Cohens d = 3.52) and NMF (Cohens d = 7.02), with p < 0.001 for both comparisons.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal mapping of ex vivo myometrial contractions in adenomyosis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveUterine dyscontractility plays a major role in pain sensation, infertility, and adenomyosis pathogenesis. In vivo, contractility occurs in the inner myometrium and junctional zone, which is thickened in adenomyosis. We examined whether the junctional zone presents particular contractile features ex vivo by measuring contractility and oxytocin response in full-thickness serosa-to-endometrium myometrial slices retrieved from control and adenomyosis patients. DesignProspective ex vivo case-control study. SubjectsPremenopausal women following hysterectomy: adenomyosis (n = 16) and controls (n = 12). Contractility: 57 strips (11 vs 8 patients), immunofluorescence: 10 vs 9 patients. Main Outcome MeasuresWe resorted to spatiotemporal mapping, time-lapse video-based techniques used in the field of gastroenterology. We measured contraction frequency, amplitude, duration, velocity, site of origin, and propagation direction along the serosa-to-endometrium axis, before and after oxytocin. We measured oxytocin receptor density along the serosa-to-endometrium axis by immunofluorescence and machine learning-assisted segmentation. ResultsEx vivo contractile waves propagated throughout the outer and inner myometrium, with similar amplitude and frequency. Contraction frequency, amplitude, duration, and velocity did not differ between control and adenomyosis uteri. Oxytocin increased contraction frequency and velocity and systematically caused contractile waves to originate at the inner myometrium in both groups. In both groups, oxytocin receptor density was highest in the inner myometrium. Adenomyosis patients had a 1.8-fold higher oxytocin receptor density, but a smaller oxytocin-induced increase in contraction frequency. ConclusionWe provide the first ex vivo spatiotemporal time-lapse analysis of myometrial contractions. The whole myometrium contracts ex vivo, not just the inner part (junctional zone). This uniform myogenic motility is presumably inhibited neurally in vivo in the outer myometrium. Ex vivo adenomyosis basal contractility was similar to that of controls. Adenomyotic myometrium overexpressed oxytocin receptors compared to controls, but this did not translate into a stronger contractile response to oxytocin. In both groups, oxytocin caused contractile waves to originate at and propagate from the sub-endometrial myometrium, where receptor density is higher. This demonstrates that contractile wave direction can be controlled hormonally.

papers.title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions
papers.abstract: BackgroundMalignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. MethodsWe applied a pre-trained deep learning model to brightfield images of single cells from malignant effusions of 10 patients with metastatic breast cancer to extract morphological features, quantify tumor cell fraction (TCF), and guide label-free microfluidic enrichment. We profiled copy-number alterations and somatic mutations in enriched tumor cell fractions and compared them with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors. ResultsAI-powered single-cell morphological analysis identified putative tumor cells in all 10 patients (median TCF, 5.4%; range, 0.51-15.8%; n = 25 samples). AI estimates of major immune-cell populations varied across patients and samples and correlated with flow cytometry measurements (n = 21 paired samples, Pearson r = 0.69-0.75). Unsupervised analysis identified four tumor cell morphotypes, revealing intra- and inter-patient morphological heterogeneity and longitudinal variation in morphotype composition. Genomic profiling of enriched tumor cell fractions by low-pass whole-genome sequencing (n = 26 samples) and whole-exome sequencing (n = 24 samples) identified copy-number alterations and somatic mutations, with tumor fraction influencing genomic signal strength. Comparisons of genomic profiles from tumor cell-enriched fractions with matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors revealed shared genomic alterations, providing orthogonal support for tumor origin and relatedness, while differences across analytes revealed genomic divergence and tumor heterogeneity. ConclusionAI-powered analysis leverages single-cell morphology for tumor cell identification and label-free enrichment, while integration with genomic profiling enables simultaneous interrogation of phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. This approach expands the potential of malignant effusions for liquid biopsy applications and biomarker development and discovery.

papers.title: HELIOS: A spatial omics-informed multi-organ cell atlas enables AI-based tumour microenvironment profiling and biomarker discovery from routine histopathology
papers.abstract: Spatial omics defines tumour microenvironments with high biological resolution but remains difficult to scale across large clinical cohorts. We developed HELIOS (H&E Learning Informed by Omics and Spatial Profiling), which transfers spatial-omics-derived cell identities into routine haematoxylin and eosin histology for interpretable single-cell tumour microenvironment profiling. HELIOS integrates 12.9 million cells from 60 specimens across 13 tissue types and four spatial profiling platforms, spanning eight epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular populations. The resulting multiclass detector generalised across independent histopathology benchmarks. Applied to colorectal, breast, and lung cancers, HELIOS recapitulated molecular subtype-associated microenvironment states and identified prognostic immune and stromal phenotypes. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes were consistently associated with favourable outcomes, whereas neutrophil and fibroblast phenotypes showed cancer-specific associations. HELIOS-derived features remained prognostic after adjustment for clinicopathological and molecular variables. These findings demonstrate that spatial omics can provide scalable biological supervision for extracting clinically relevant tumour microenvironment features from routine H&E, supporting scalable risk stratification and biomarker development across clinical cohorts and retrospective pathology archives.

papers.title: Predicting HPV/p16 Status and Molecular Subtypes from Histopathology Slides using Deep Learning in Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) comprises three prognostically distinct molecular subtypes: human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated, HPV-independent/p53-wildtype, and HPV-independent/p53-abnormal. Classification requires p16/p53 immunohistochemistry, which consumes tissue and is often incomplete in retrospective cohorts. We investigated whether deep learning could predict HPV/p16 status and molecular subtypes directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. Using features extracted with H-optimus-1, we developed two attention-based multiple-instance learning models: HERA, predicting HPV/p16 status, and HERMES, predicting the three molecular subtypes. Models were developed on 644 patients from three Dutch VSCC cohorts and tested on 286 patients from two independent cohorts. In independent testing, HERA achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.75-0.91), with specificity 0.93, negative predictive value 0.94, and sensitivity 0.68. HERA-predicted groups reproduced the prognostic separation of HPV testing (log-rank p<0.001). HERMES achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.70 (0.66-0.75), with good discrimination for HPV-associated (0.80) but limited separation of HPV-independent/p53-abnormal (AUC 0.68) and HPV-independent/p53-wildtype (AUC 0.63). HERMES-predicted classes reproduced the prognostic hierarchy, with 5-year recurrence rates of 14.0% (HPV-associated), 31.1% (HPV-independent/p53-wildtype) and 43.3% (HPV-independent/p53-abnormal) (p=0.0051). Highly attended tiles showed basaloid cells and koilocytotic-like atypia in HPV-associated tumors, keratinizing nests with desmoplastic stroma in HPV-independent/p53-abnormal tumors, and well-differentiated keratinocytes with spongiosis in HPV-independent/p53-wildtype tumors. HERA could assign HPV/p16 status to large retrospective VSCC cohorts lacking ancillary testing, without consuming tissue, enabling HPV-stratified outcome analyses. Before such use, external validation of its discrimination and calibration across scanners and populations is required. HERMES suggests that molecular subtype information is encoded in hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, but requires improved distinction between the HPV-independent subtypes.

papers.title: AI-Enhanced Segmentation and Scoring of Histopathological Growth Patterns in Resected Colorectal Liver Metastases
papers.abstract: Histopathological growth patterns, predominantly the presence of an encapsulated rim, serve as powerful prognostic biomarkers in colorectal liver metastases. However, conventional visual estimation is limited by interobserver variability, human rounding bias, and categorical thresholds. We aimed to develop and externally validate a deep-learning segmentation framework that produces continuous, spatially resolved, and objective encapsulation metrics from routine whole-slide images. In this multicenter study of chemo-naive resected CRLM patients, a modified nnU-Net architecture was developed on 40 pixel-annotated H&E-stained WSIs to segment liver parenchyma, tumor, and the encapsulation interface. Model performance was optimized across spatial resolutions. An automated continuous AI encapsulation score was computed to determine patient-level metrics. The prognostic value for 5-year overall survival was evaluated using restricted cubic spline Cox regression, a log-rank optimized threshold, and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses across a main cohort (Erasmus MC; n = 546, 1,910 WSIs) and an independent external validation cohort (Radboud UMC; n = 212, 615 WSIs). The segmentation network achieved optimal tissue boundary delineation at a resolution of 2.0 {micro}m/pixel on the 40 annotated slides (overall foreground DICE: 0.86 {+/-} 0.09; encapsulation DICE: 0.70 {+/-} 0.11). Spline modeling demonstrated that while visual assessment displayed non-linear hazard plateaus, the continuous AI encapsulation score exhibited a linear reduction in mortality risk across the critical intermediate range (25%-75% encapsulation, p = 7.81 x 10-4). Log-rank optimization identified a primary global threshold at 47.4% (p = 3.73 x 10-8), which in confirmed significant OS stratification in external validation (p = 0.018). A secondary threshold was found at 69% (p = 2.93 x 10-6) that captured high-encapsulation favorable-risk patients matching the current manual 100% Rotterdam cut-off. Our deep-learning model transforms qualitative HGP grading into a continuous, explainable, and fully automated prognostic biometry. By eliminating observer subjectivity and capturing fine-grained risk gradients, the model establishes a scalable, standardized foundation for CRLM risk stratification on digital pathology.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology in Thyroid Diseases: Comparison with Histopathological Findings in Hawassa, Ethiopia
papers.abstract: IntroductionThyroid diseases are major health problems and among the most common endocrine disorders worldwide, including in Ethiopia. They are characterized by alterations in hormone secretion, enlargement of the thyroid gland, or both. Fine needle aspiration cytology is an important initial screening tool, and histopathologic examination is essential for the definitive diagnosis of thyroid disease. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology with histopathology in identifying thyroid diseases. MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted at three health facilities in Hawassa City, Ethiopia, involving 304 patients who underwent both thyroid fine needle aspiration cytology and histopathologic examination of the same site between 30th October 2024 and 29th October 2025. FNAC results were classified using the Bethesda system, with histopathology as the gold standard. Data were entered into Kobo Toolbox, exported to SPSS version 27, and analyzed using cross-tabulation and chi-square ({chi}2) tests to determine diagnostic accuracy. Result304 patient records were included in the study. The fine needle aspiration cytology was determinate/diagnostic in 81.6% of cases. The study revealed the sensitivity and specificity of fine needle aspiration cytology to be 88.2% (CI 77.6-95.1%) and 94.4% (CI 90.6-97.1%), respectively. The false negative and false positive rates in this study were 2.4% and 4.4%, respectively. The positive predictive value was 80.3% (CI 68.7-89.3%), and the negative predictive value was 96.8% (CI 93.8-98.7%). The accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology in differentiating benign from malignant thyroid lesions was 93.1%. ConclusionFNAC demonstrated strong agreement with histopathology and remains a reliable, cost-effective first-line diagnostic tool for thyroid disease, particularly in resource-limited settings. Strengthening sample handling, ultrasound guidance, and adherence to Bethesda criteria may further improve diagnostic precision

papers.title: CytoLens: a modular deep learning system for quantitative cervical cytology
papers.abstract: Cervical cytology screening relies on the visual assessment of nuclear and cellular morphology across thousands of cells per slide, a labor-intensive task that could benefit from quantitative computational support. Here we present CytoLens, a modular deep learning system that detects and counts nuclei, delineates nuclei and whole cells, measures the nuclear-to-cell area ratio (N:C), classifies cells from multifocal images and scores candidate abnormality. We trained and tested each module on a public dataset matched to its task, without pooling datasets. CytoLens detected nuclei with an F1 score of 0.931 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.914-0.946) and counted 75 of 100 fields to within one nucleus. Point-prompted segmentation achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.901 for nuclei and 0.847 for whole cells and, without retraining, transferred to a second dataset in which measured N:C increased with lesion grade in parallel with expert outlines. Multifocal hierarchical classification reached a mean accuracy of 0.947 across four Bethesda-aligned categories, and abnormality scores ranked annotated abnormal candidates with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.865. These results support the evaluation of CytoLens on patient-linked clinical specimens.

papers.title: Peritumoral SULF1 Transcript Signal Is Associated with Disease-Specific Survival in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: The prognostic relevance of peritumoral SULF1 transcript signal in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is unclear. We assembled a retrospective cohort of 133 patients with 218 primary-site tissue-microarray cores; 131 patients had evaluable boundary features. Multiplex fluorescence imaging combined RNAscope SULF1, CK-pan, and DAPI. Tumor-stroma boundaries were annotated with the SULF1 channel hidden. We screened 50 exported boundary features across cumulative stromal bands of 35-300 m against recurrence-free survival (RFS), overall survival (OS), and disease-specific survival (DSS), with false-discovery-rate correction. The strongest DSS association was signal SD within 150 m (n = 107; 23 disease-specific deaths; HR = 2.20 per SD; 95% CI, 1.64-2.94; q = 2.1 x 10-). In 50 repeated 5-fold cross-validations with feature selection repeated within training folds, adding a boundary feature to AJCC stage increased mean held-out DSS c-index from 0.613 to 0.754 ({Delta}C = +0.141; 2.5th-97.5th percentiles across repeats, +0.105 to +0.192). These percentiles describe split variability, not confidence intervals. The 150-m SD feature was selected in 39.2% of DSS training folds. The DSS association persisted after adjustment for mean signal, although the measurements were strongly correlated. Peritumoral SULF1 signal dispersion was associated with outcome beyond an ordinal AJCC-stage model; independent validation is required.

papers.title: Large Language Models for Structured Information Extraction from German Histopathology Reports - Hepatocellular Carcinoma
papers.abstract: BackgroundClinical registries and institutional quality control (QC) in pathology heavily depend on complex histopathological data. However, critical tumor characteristics are mostly locked in unstructured free-text reports. We hypothesize that locally deployed, resource-eWicient language models operating within a secure institutional network can reliably extract relevant variables from German reports of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), thereby enabling automated data curation without transferring sensitive patient data. MethodsWe developed a local, privacy-preserving open-weight Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline consisting of two consecutive stages: Stage 1 utilizes a lightweight gatekeeper model to isolate the target cohort of confirmed Hepatocellular Carcinoma cases from a screening pool of N = 2,864 reports. Stage 2 deploys a high-capacity model to extract 15 predefined histopathological variables, including tumor-node-metastasis staging, histological grading, vascular invasion, and selected immunohistochemical features into structured JSON format. For both Stages, pipeline performance was evaluated using Accuracy, Macro F1-scores, and Cohens kappa compared to expert-curated reference annotations. ResultsThe top-performing Stage 1 gatekeeper isolated the target patient cohort with zero classification errors, effectively reaching complete agreement with the reference standard (ground truth) and correcting inaccurate administrative metadata. For Stage 2 feature extraction, current-generation models demonstrated robust structural reliability, reducing the burden of manual post-processing. The 31B model configuration (Gemma 4) virtually eliminated objective factual errors, achieving near-perfect agreement with the reference standard (Macro F1 > 0.99). ConclusionLocal two-stage pipelines offer a highly accurate, resource-efficient, and secure solution for clinical text processing. This framework serves as a privacy-preserving engine for institutional quality control and the scalable curation of pathology registries.

papers.title: An interpretable cell-centric representation of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma matches multiple-instance learning for clinical outcomes and leads to novel pathologist-driven histological biomarkers
papers.abstract: Current state of the art computational pathology foundation models attain satisfying accuracy most general pathology tasks including detection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) but fail to provide sufficient explainability, operating as "black boxes". Some interpretability effort has been made, with models providing attention maps that project back on the slide the models high attended areas that pushed for the given prediction result, without further naming or reasoning explanation which can limit pathologists trust toward the prediction. We developed C3PRO, a cell-centric framework attempting to provide deeper understanding and explainability, by using embeddings extracted using a pathology foundation model, from cell centered tiles containing both the cell and its close neighborhood, which were then clustered into recurrent morphological phenotypes. A spatial graph was additionally constructed on top of the back-projected vocabulary to account for recurrent motifs. The evaluation of the model performance involved a cohort of 809 patients (825 diagnostic biopsies) using nested cross validation. C3PRO was benchmarked against four different multiple instance learning frameworks and achieved on-par performance for diagnostic (0.958 AUC), survival (0.617) and resectability (0.696) prediction, while providing additional insights compared to the strongest baseline models. Each clustered phenotype was probed and extracted as a representative tile mosaic and annotated by two expert pathologists, constituting a phenotype vocabulary available for statistical analysis. These phenotypes were scored by pathologists with physical brightfield microscopy and replicated the independent statistical significance impact on overall survival prediction from diagnostic biopsies. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCEPathology foundation model multiple-instance-learning frameworks cannot be audited by the pathologists. We demonstrate that a representation constructed from identifiable cell phenotypes is on par with state-of-the-art models for diagnosis, prognosis, and resectability in pancreatic cancer. This approach also uncovers prognostic stromal states that expert observers cannot differentiate using light microscopy.

papers.title: Benchmarking modular skills and fixed orchestration across six large language models in a meta-analysis task
papers.abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support systematic review and meta-analysis, but complex evidence flow, trial-family identification, study-level data extraction, and statistical execution remain vulnerable to omissions, untraceable data paths, and scientifically flawed steps. It remains unclear whether gains are driven by modular skills or by fixed orchestration, and whether these effects differ across base models. MethodsWe conducted a controlled, multi-model benchmark in which six LLMs completed the same randomized controlled trial (RCT) meta-analysis task under three conditions: (A) no meta-analysis-specific skills; (B) autonomous access to modular meta-analysis skills; and (C) the same skills executed under a Quality-First fixed directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each model was run three times per condition (54 runs total). The primary outcome was the scientific performance score (SPS, 0-100), rated by two meta-analysis experts; one expert was masked to explicit model and condition labels during SPS scoring, and final scores were the arithmetic mean of the two raters. Inter-rater reliability was high (SPS ICC(A,2) = 0.991). ResultsMean SPS was 43.50 (condition A), 55.65 (B), and 54.44 (C). Relative to unassisted models, modular skills improved mean SPS by +12.15 points (unadjusted 95% CI 3.15-21.16; Holm-adjusted P = 0.033). The combined modular-skills-plus-fixed-DAG condition showed a positive but not statistically significant difference relative to unassisted models (C - A = +10.94; Holm-adjusted P = 0.073) and no incremental gain over skills alone (C - B = - 1.21; Holm-adjusted P = 0.746). No condition-by-model interaction was detected (P = 0.801). ConclusionsIn this benchmark task, access to modular skills improved mean scientific performance relative to unassisted execution; fixed orchestration of the same skills did not provide a detectable incremental benefit. The findings are task-specific and do not establish general effects for other meta-analysis settings, models, or orchestration designs.

papers.title: Errors, Hallucinations, and Clinical Impact of General-Purpose Multimodal Large Language Models in Histopathology
papers.abstract: BackgroundGeneral-purpose large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated in diagnostic pathology, but prior studies have largely emphasized diagnostic accuracy rather than how models fail. We evaluated four LLMs for diagnostic performance, pathology-relevant errors and hallucinations, their burden, and potential clinical impact across multi-organ pathology cases. DesignIn this retrospective multicenter study, 153 pathology cases from two institutions spanning 20 organs were evaluated using ChatGPT-5.3 (LLM1), Gemini 3 (LLM2), Grok 4.20 (LLM3), and Claude Opus 4.6 (LLM4). Each LLM received multi-magnification histologic images with clinical context and generated a microscopic description and diagnosis. No data splitting, training, or fine-tuning was performed. Twenty-one pathologists assessed 612 outputs for diagnostic correctness, error and hallucination type and burden, clinical impact (0-4), and overall performance (1-5). ResultsStrict diagnostic accuracy was 48.9% overall (60.1% including partially correct diagnoses) and ranged from 36.6% to 58.2% across LLMs. Errors occurred in 82.0% of outputs and hallucinations in 76.6%; 90.2% contained at least one error or hallucination. Misinterpretation was the most frequent error (72.1%), while fabricated histologic features were the dominant hallucination type (74.5%). LLM2 had significantly lower misinterpretation rates than the other three LLMs, while LLM3 had significantly higher fabricated-feature hallucination rates than LLM1 and LLM2. Errors were more frequent in incorrect than correct diagnoses (97.5% vs 66.2%), as were hallucinations (95.1% vs 59.9%; both p < 0.001). Every strictly incorrect diagnosis contained an error and/or hallucination, while 79.9% of strictly correct diagnoses also contained at least one. In multivariable analysis, LLM3 was independently associated with higher odds of an incorrect diagnosis. Diagnostic correctness was the strongest determinant of high clinical impact; each one-point increase in hallucination burden increased the odds by 63% (adjusted OR, 1.63). ConclusionDiagnostic accuracy alone substantially underestimates the safety limitations of general-purpose LLMs in histopathology. Errors and hallucinations were common even when the final diagnosis was correct, and their burden was independently associated with clinical impact. Evaluation frameworks should therefore assess both diagnostic correctness and the reliability and potential consequences of accompanying generated content.

papers.title: Distinct Evolutionary Trajectories in Early Lung Adenocarcinoma: Age-Related Pathway with Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor-Associated Genome Doubling and Smoking-Driven Pathway
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT/SUMMARYLung adenocarcinoma a progress from preinvasive lesions to invasive cancer; however, early evolutionary events in adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (MIA) remain poorly defined, particularly in East Asian populations enriched for EGFR mutations. We performed whole-exome sequencing on 67 Japanese patients (38 AIS, 29 MIA), including multiregion sampling in 13 cases to identify EGFR as predominant driver (61.2%), followed by RBM10 (19.4%) and TP53 (9.0%). Two evolutionary trajectories emerged: age-related and smoking-driven pathways. In the former, EGFR mutant tumors frequently exhibited early whole genome doubling (WGD) (24.4%) with clock like signature. The smoking driven pathway, typically involving KRAS mutations, displayed a tobacco associated signature. Multiregion sequencing revealed that driver mutations (EGFR, KRAS, and MET) were shared trunk events across in situ and invasive regions, while secondary alterations arose subclonally. This study defines the genomic evolution of early lung adenocarcinoma in Japanese patients, identifying two evolutionary trajectories: an age-related pathway with EGFR-linked genome doubling and a smoking-driven pathway involving KRAS mutations. These findings elucidate mechanisms underlying progression from preinvasive lesions to invasive cancer in Asian populations.

papers.title: PRECISE: Benchmarking digital pathology with expert-annotated contiguous IHC-H&E serial prostate sections
papers.abstract: We present PRECISE (PRostate Expert-annotated Contiguous IHC-H&E Serial sEctions), a hybrid histopathology dataset of paired hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) whole-slide images (WSIs), comprising 37 prostate core needle biopsies from 25 patients, each with matched H&E and CKAPM+racemase staining. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first publicly available dataset offering spatially harmonized, pixel-level expert annotations across both staining modalities in prostate biopsy WSIs -- directly mirroring the two-stage (H&E-then-IHC) clinical diagnostic workflow used to resolve morphological uncertainty, restricted to cases in which that workflow reached diagnostic consensus. The dataset contains 24,387 annotations spanning seven diagnostically critical classes: malignant glands, benign glands, stromal tissue, intraductal carcinoma (IDC-P), high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN), atypical intraductal proliferation (AIP), and tissue artifacts. Unlike existing resources, which focus on binary tumor classification or lack IHC pairing, this dataset captures the full morphological spectrum encountered in routine prostate pathology, including rare precursor lesions and confounding entities underrepresented in current benchmarks. Annotations were validated through a structured three-stage consensus by two expert uropathologists, with IHC serving as biological ground truth for boundary definition. PRECISE is designed as a robust benchmark for multimodal semantic segmentation and self-supervised learning, and is openly released to promote reproducible research and accelerate AI-assisted diagnosis in prostate cancer. Our dataset is available at 10.5281/zenodo.20721779.

papers.title: Host-related concordance of TAC/SARIFA in colorectal double and triple carcinomas suggests patient-specific metabolic reprogramming
papers.abstract: IntroductionTAC/SARIFA has been introduced as a new robust and easy to evaluate biomarker in several cancer entities including colorectal cancer. It is defined by a direct contact of at least five tumour cells with one adipocyte and is believed to indicate metabolic reprogramming associated with adverse outcome. However, the mechanism that leads to TAC/SARIFA-positivity is unclear, yet. To investigate whether there is an individuals component we conducted a study on double and triple cancer establishing a within-patient-design. MethodsWe retrospectively analysed a total number of 135 cases with 276 col-orectal cancers from two academic medical centres. The TAC/SARIFA status was evaluated as well as the basic histopathological factors. The median follow-up time was 120 months. ResultsCases with any TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours showed a significant reduced overall survival (62 v s. 88 months; p = 0 .011). Analysing the entire cohort the rates of concordant and discordant cases followed a random distribution. However, restriction to synchronous pT3/4-cases revealed a significant (p = 0.016) deviation from a random distribution. ConclusionThis study reveals significant concordance of TAC/SARIFA status in synchronous locally advanced colorectal double/triple carcinomas, supporting the concept that tumour-adipocyte interaction reflects a host-related microenvironmental condition linked to metabolic reprogramming rather than a purely tumour-intrinsic event.

papers.title: Standardized, repeatable ulcerative colitis histology scoring and endpoint assessment using an automated, foundation model-based tool
papers.abstract: In clinical trials for ulcerative colitis (UC), pathologists assess disease severity through standardized histological indices, including the Geboes Score, Robarts Histopathology Index (RHI), and Nancy Histologic Index (NHI). Despite strong associations with clinical outcomes, histologic scoring suffers from inter- and intra-reader variability, and consensus criteria for histologic remission remain uncertain. Through a consortium approach, we developed an artificial intelligence-based measurement (AIM) tool for scoring histology in UC mucosal biopsies (AIM-HI UC). This model, trained on a large dataset of UC biopsies (N=10,230), utilizes additive multiple instance learning models leveraging PLUTO, a pathology foundation model, that predict each of the Geboes subgrades, from which the Geboes grade-level score, RHI, and NHI can be calculated. Evaluation of this model on a standalone verification set including clinical trial specimens established algorithm non-inferiority and/or superiority relative to standard qualified pathologists through comparison of algorithm-consensus and pathologist-consensus agreement metrics (non-inferior if difference >-0.1, superior if difference >0, inclusive of confidence intervals). AIM-HI UC was determined to be non-inferior to pathologists (N=3) for the prediction of all seven Geboes subgrades, grade-level Geboes, RHI, NHI, histologic improvement (GS<3.1), 2A histologic remission (GS<2A.0), and 2B histologic remission (GS<2B.0). AIM-HI UC was superior to pathologists for several Geboes subgrades (GS 0, GS 1, GS 2B, and GS 5), as well as grade-level Geboes, RHI, and positive percent agreement of 2A histologic remission. The model was shown to be greater than 99% repeatable for all histologic scoring metrics examined. Model-derived scores were shown to strongly correlate with canonical histologic features of inflammation, including the proportion of total epithelium that is inflamed (Spearman r=0.83; p<0.01), the proportion of neutrophils localized within crypt epithelium (Spearman r=0.83, p<0.01), and the amount of mucosal area classified as erosion or ulceration (Spearman r=0.80, p<0.01). Overall, these results suggest that AIM-HI UC has the potential to improve consistency of UC histology interpretation, providing a path toward standardization of UC histology scoring in clinical trials.

papers.title: Association of white matter hyperintensities, white matter microstructural changes, hippocampal and amygdala volumes with neuropathology in a community cohort using 7T postmortem in situ MRI
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONWe integrate visual and quantitative metrics in white matter and medial temporal lobe to examine relationships with neuropathology in a community cohort. METHODSPostmortem in situ MRI (T1, T2, DWI) was performed in 25 human brains, followed by visual ratings (Fazekas, MTA, ERICA, Koedam). Neuropathology included ADNC, LATE-NC, hippocampal sclerosis, PART, ARTAG, Lewy pathology, and CAA. RESULTSIncreased Fazekas score was linked to aging, lower education, hypertension, higher basilar artery wall thickness, and greater Braak NFT stage. WMH volume also correlated with lacunes, Thal phase, and CERAD score that was not observed using Fazekas. Hippocampal volumes were lower in elderly, less educated people and were associated with higher atrophy scores and higher Braak NFT stage. Higher amygdala volume was only associated with higher CERAD score. DISCUSSIONQuantitative MRI may detect neuropathologic associations more sensitively than visual ratings. Tau pathology is a key predictor of WMH burden and hippocampal atrophy.

papers.title: A multicenter Swedish histopathology image dataset of pediatric central nervous system tumors
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWRefined detection methods, more detailed tumor characterization, and adequate distinction between different pediatric tumor subtypes are necessary to improve diagnosis and treatment, enable precision medicine, and advance patient prognosis. However, the application of computational approaches to pediatric brain tumors remains limited, largely due to the lack of accessible datasets. To address part of this gap, we provide whole slide images (WSIs) of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue sections from pediatric central nervous system (CNS) samples collected in Sweden in 2013 to 2023. These data represent a population-based national cohort encompassing all six pediatric oncology centers in Sweden and are available through the Swedish Childhood Tumor Biobank (BTB). The dataset includes 1,446 WSIs of sufficient image quality with confirmed CNS tumor diagnoses, derived from 537 unique subjects (562 subject-diagnosis pair cases). In addition, diagnostic-relevant clinical information is included. Corresponding whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-transcriptome sequencing (WTS), and methylation array data are available upon application for most tumor samples through separate resources at BTB. This H&E dataset has been specifically curated to support artificial intelligence-based analyses, while also serving broader applications in medical research and education. When combined with matched molecular data, it provides a valuable resource for advancing multimodal and precision diagnostic approaches in the pediatric population.

papers.title: An Automated, Pathologist-free Gleason Grade Stratifies Disease-free Interval Comparably to Expert Grading from a Single Out-of-distribution Slide
papers.abstract: Automated Gleason grading now matches expert pathologists on the cohorts where systems are developed and tuned, but deployment-relevant gaps remain: whether an automated grade, applied without site-specific tuning or pathologist oversight, stratifies outcome comparably to expert grading on slides from unseen institutions and in cross-specimen applications. We tested this for disease-free interval (DFI), a curated recurrence endpoint. A production gland-level prostate diagnostic (PathTools Prostate v11.0) was applied frozen and uncalibrated to 298 diagnostic whole-slide images from 274 TCGA-PRAD radical-prostatectomy patients, a cohort outside its development distribution and needle-core-biopsy training data, contributed by 25 source sites under heterogeneous digitization; tissue was detected automatically with no expert region annotation. From the output we derived an ISUP grade group and continuous high-grade content, and evaluated each grade as a standalone predictor of DFI (24 events) by Harrells c-index with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, a paired between-method bootstrap, and Kaplan-Meier curves with the log-rank test. The automated grade reproduced the clinical grade group at quadratic-weighted {kappa} = 0.62 (95% CI 0.53-0.70; 48% exact, 86% within one group), within the expert inter-observer range. As the sole predictor it stratified recurrence (log-rank p = 0.022; c-index 0.69, 95% CI 0.58-0.79), and the continuous high-grade fraction was robustly prognostic (hazard ratio 1.37 per SD, p = 0.029; c-index 0.71, 0.61-0.81). Standalone discrimination was not statistically separable from the clinical grade (c-index 0.78, 0.69-0.86; paired {Delta} c-index spanning zero), and in a joint model the automated grade added nothing beyond it, consistent with both measuring a shared morphological axis. From a single out-of-distribution slide with no pathologist oversight, the automated grade provides standalone recurrence stratification not statistically separable from whole-gland expert grading, demonstrating robust generalizability beyond training data; reported as a continuous high-grade fraction, it offers reproducible, expert-free, grade-equivalent risk stratification for harmonizing large archival or genomically-profiled cohorts.

papers.title: DeepSpot-M: a multimodal foundation model for transcriptome-wide virtual spatial transcriptomics from histology
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics remains costly and low-throughput, limiting it to a small fraction of routine histology and leaving the molecular state of disease unmeasured in most patients. Predicting spatial expression from histology could address this gap, but existing methods are restricted to predefined genes and small cohorts. We present DeepSpot-M, a multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial expression by representing genes with embeddings from foundation models spanning DNA, RNA, proteins, single cells and biomedical text. By reformulating prediction as a query over genes, DeepSpot-M spans the protein-coding transcriptome and predicts genes unseen during training. Trained on a large pan-cancer dataset, it transfers to held-out cancers, outperforming specialised models trained on them, and adapts to new cohorts and single-cell assays from one slide via test-time adaptation. Applied to TCGA, it generates a virtual atlas of 28,664 slides across 32 cancers, recovering a pan-cancer map of malignancy from histology. The same query interface further enables transcriptome restoration, cross-species non-coding RNA inference, in silico variant-effect mapping and natural-language querying. We anticipate DeepSpot-M will provide a scalable foundation for virtual spatial transcriptomics and biomarker discovery.
